facts.claim: Tim Barry's "Avoiding Catatonic Surrender" is track 2 on the album Rivanna Junction, released November 21, 2006, and runs 3:36.
Discogs credits Tim Barry as producer and writer of the album. Lance Koehler is credited as engineer and producer, and Joe Mager as assistant engineer.
On this track Tim Barry sings and plays guitar, and Caitlin Barry plays violin. The violin credit is annotated as one take, drunk and not in tune.
Discogs credits the album's song titles as lifted from quotes by Buz Blurr.
Rivanna Junction was recorded in July 2006 at Minimum Wage Studio in Richmond, VA.

AllMusic's review singles out the stark "Avoiding Catatonic Surrender" for its lyric about hating Republicans, Democrats and liberals alike, and for its self-contradictions about violence and pacifism.
Rivanna Junction first came out in 2006 on Suburban Home Records (SBH 038CD). Chunksaah Records reissued it in 2011 (CAR047).
Barry took two weeks off in 2006 to record the album, using friends and family as backing musicians. He moved to Chunksaah for 2008's Manchester.
Barry recalled that his father listened to Rivanna Junction and asked if he was alright because there was a lot of pain on it. Barry said he was, because he had gotten it out.
Tim Barry is from Richmond, Virginia, and is the lead singer of the punk band Avail. He has performed folk music on his own since 2004.

research.lineage: Barry's solo work is stripped-down, Woody Guthrie-inspired folk from a Richmond, Virginia punk and hardcore background (Avail), and it is often described as folk-punk.

draft:
The song opens with Tim Barry muttering that he hates it. Before the first verse he's already called it a pain in his ass, and the rest of **Avoiding Catatonic Surrender** keeps arguing with itself the same way. The first scene is a Motel 6 in East Brunswick, New Jersey: cigarettes until the lungs burn, ice in the trash can to keep the beer cold. Then comes the detail that turns a road complaint into something lonelier: "Breathe in the perfume in the room of the person last here." He's alone, and the closest thing to company is the scent a stranger left behind.

The feeling isn't homesickness. It's the trap of "I can't stand being home, lord, I can't stand being gone," where neither place brings relief and the restlessness has nowhere to land. His ears ring in the quiet. He'd call somebody, but he has nothing to say. It's a specific kind of tired, where loneliness and the wish to be left alone share the same body.

The second verse goes back to a one-night thing: sex on the couch, a morning spent pretending it didn't happen, her lost phone dug out from under their clothes, then a 15-hour shift for barely a hundred bucks. He shrugs it off. Anything that starts is bound to end. But he also wishes he'd kept his eyes closed, and that wish gives away how much the shrug is covering.

Verse three throws out any idea of a tidy self. He throws beer cans at the TV news and sneers at Republicans, Democrats, and liberals in one breath. Then: "I think pacifists are weak and violence is wrong." He goes limp for police and fights when it's called for. The song doesn't resolve any of it. The pride in belonging nowhere sits right beside the plain admission that he doesn't know where he'd fit if he tried.

The sound is as bare as the confession. Strummed acoustic guitar and a walking bass keep a relaxed, steady folk-rock gait, and a harmonica threads lines between the vocal phrases. Barry's voice is raspy and conversational, with no harmonies, and the recording is left raw. It's the Woody Guthrie model run through a Richmond punk lifer, the singer of Avail, and he mocks the form from inside it, calling these boring standard songs built on boring standard chords. Caitlin Barry's violin is credited as one take, drunk and not in tune, which tells you how much polish was the goal.

Barry's father heard the album and asked if he was alright, because there was so much pain on it. Barry said he was, because he'd gotten it out. The chorus keeps saying so long and insisting he can't keep singing these songs, even as he sings it again and again. That contradiction is the hook: you hear someone swearing off the only thing that's keeping him upright.
